summary: The note is a Wikipedia article on pumped-storage hydroelectricity (PSH), an electric energy storage method that pumps water from a lower reservoir to a higher one when power is cheap and releases it through turbines during peak demand. It covers the basic principle, efficiency and economics, small-scale and historical development, and worldwide capacity figures, including the largest operational plants. The captured text is cut off partway through the table of the five largest plants.
one_line: Wikipedia article describing pumped-storage hydroelectricity, a grid energy storage method using elevation-based water reservoirs, its efficiency, history, and global capacity.
key_facts: Pumped-storage hydroelectricity (PSH), also called pumped hydroelectric energy storage (PHES), stores energy as gravitational potential energy of water pumped from a lower reservoir to a higher one.
Round-trip energy efficiency of PSH varies between 70%–80%, with some sources claiming up to 87%.
PSH accounts for around 95% of all active tracked storage installations worldwide, per the United States Department of Energy Global Energy Storage Database as of 2020.
Worldwide PSH total installed throughput capacity is over 181 GW, of which about 29 GW are in the United States.
The global greenfield pumped hydro atlas lists more than 600,000 potential sites worldwide, about 100 times more than needed to support 100% renewable electricity.
The Snowy 2.0 scheme in Australia, under construction, uses existing reservoirs (dubbed "bluefield") and has a 350 Gigawatt-hour storage capacity.
Water requirements for PSH are about 1 gigalitre of initial fill water per gigawatt-hour of storage, and land requirements are about 10 hectares per gigawatt-hour.
The first use of pumped storage was in 1907 in Switzerland, at the Engeweiher pumped storage facility near Schaffhausen.

The first use of pumped storage in the United States was in 1930 by the Connecticut Electric and Power Company, pumping water from the Housatonic River to a reservoir 70 metres (230 ft) above, near New Milford, Connecticut.
In 2009, world pumped storage generating capacity was 104 GW, while other sources claim 127 GW.
In 2010 the United States had 21.5 GW of pumped storage generating capacity, 20.6% of world capacity.
Nameplate pumped storage capacity in the United States had grown to 21.6 GW by 2014, comprising 97% of grid-scale energy storage in the United States.
Reversible turbine/generator assemblies act as combined pump and turbine generator units, usually Francis turbine designs.
The Ffestiniog Pumped Storage Scheme in North Wales has four water turbines generating 360 MW of electricity within 60 seconds of the need arising.
Pumped storage plants have a proven long service life of decades, in some cases over a century, which is three to five times longer than utility-scale batteries.
Closed loop (off-river) pumped hydro storage has the smallest carbon emissions per unit of storage of all candidates for large-scale energy storage.
